lore_summary.en: What the sword cannot keep, words can. Ferdowsi's testament to the power of Persian memory.
lore_summary.fa: پس از فتح عرب، فارسی از دربارها عقب نشست اما در خانه‌ها، شعر شفاهی و کوهستان‌ها زنده ماند. با دولت‌های سامانی در قرن نهم و دهم، فارسی به عنوان یک کنش سیاسی و فرهنگی بازگشت. فردوسی وارث این بازیابی بود — شاهنامه‌ای نوشت که ثابت کرد حافظه بر شمشیر پیروز می‌شود.

scenes.body_en: Swords rust. Empires end. Armies forget what they fought for within three generations. Memory is more durable than any of these, but only if someone tends it — only if, in each generation, someone decides that the work of remembering is worth doing even when no one is paying for it and no court is asking for it and the language you are preserving has been officially replaced by another.

After the Arab conquest, Persian did not disappear. It retreated — into households, into oral poetry, into the mountains and the eastern provinces where Arabic administration had arrived but not yet taken root in the culture. When the Abbasid caliphate gave way to regional dynasties, and when those regional dynasties began looking for ways to express their own identities, Persian came back. The Samanid rulers of Khorasan in the ninth and tenth centuries patronized Persian poetry deliberately, as a political and cultural act. The language returned to courts and chanceries. It carried with it everything that had been stored in it during the two centuries of official Arabic dominance.

This was the world Ferdowsi was born into — a Persian revival that had been building for a hundred years before he put his pen to paper. He did not invent the recovery. He completed it. The Shahnameh was the culmination of the Samanid project, the work that proved Persian could sustain a monument of the scale that Arabic had achieved in the Quran, that the old stories had not been forgotten, that the civilization that the conquest had interrupted was still present in the language and the memory of the people who spoke it.

Memory won. Not by fighting — the swords were gone — but by the simple act of being told again, and again, and again, until the telling became the tradition and the tradition became the identity and the identity became stronger than any army that had ever tried to replace it.

battle.intro_en: The sword takes empires. Words keep civilizations. To face this gate you must hold Ferdowsi's central argument: that the Shahnameh itself is the act of preservation.
battle.intro_fa: شمشیر امپراتوری‌ها را می‌گیرد. کلمات تمدن‌ها را نگه می‌دارند. برای مواجهه با این دروازه باید استدلالِ محوریِ فردوسی را نگه داری: که خودِ شاهنامه عملِ نگهداری است.
